section_summary: This section documents the Department of State's diplomatic correspondence, intelligence coordination, and operational efforts between late September and late October 1945 to locate, impound, and examine Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and assets worldwide following the surrender of Japan. It details inter-Allied negotiations and jurisdictional friction regarding French exclusion from archival seizures in the Levant, coordination among the Big Four powers (United States, Great Britain, Soviet Union, and China), and administrative stalemates stemming from General Douglas MacArthur's delay in issuing formal surrender instructions to Japanese overseas missions. Additionally, the section includes comprehensive intelligence inventories of recovered Japanese records and espionage files from Panama, El Salvador, and Ecuador, as well as high-level diplomatic policy discussions with the British Embassy regarding global archival preservation and examination.

subfiles.about: The French Government protests its exclusion from the Allied seizure of Japanese diplomatic archives and property in the Levant and requests participation.
subfiles.summary: The French Embassy delivers Aide-Mémoire No. 771 noting that the French Delegate General in the Levant was informed by US Minister George Wadsworth that US, British, Soviet, and Chinese representatives obtained Japanese archives from the Spanish Consulate in Beirut and intend to sequester Japanese property in Syria and Lebanon. France expresses surprise and dissatisfaction at being excluded from these actions without prior consultation. It requests that Wadsworth be instructed to associate the French representative with these steps immediately and asks for broader information on American plans regarding the disposition of Japanese assets abroad.
subfiles.title: French Embassy Aide-Mémoire No. 771 on Seizure of Japanese Archives and Property in the Levant

subfiles.about: Department routing slip transmitting the French Embassy aide-mémoire for translation and action.
subfiles.from: Mary Gass (Translating Section, Division of Central Services)
subfiles.summary: This routing slip sends the French Embassy's aide-mémoire No. 771 to Adrian B. Colquitt in the Division of Near Eastern Affairs with a request to translate and return it. A telephone note added on September 26, 1945, indicates that Colquitt requested the translation be forwarded instead to Oscar S. Straus in the Foreign Activity Correlation Division (FC).
subfiles.title: State Department Routing Slip Regarding French Aide-Mémoire
subfiles.to: Adrian B. Colquitt (NE), redirected to Oscar S. Straus (FC)

subfiles.about: US representative to the Holy See reports the Vatican considers the Japanese Embassy's status unchanged and no surrender orders have been received.
subfiles.summary: Tittmann reports that the Vatican states the Japanese Ambassador to the Holy See has received no instructions from Tokyo regarding handing over archives and property to the Allies. The Vatican considers the status of the Japanese Embassy unchanged despite Japan's surrender, as demonstrated by the Ambassador being received in a private audience by Pope Pius XII on September 25. Tittmann requests State Department guidance and comments on this anomalous diplomatic situation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 201 from Vatican City on Status of Japanese Embassy to the Holy See

subfiles.about: Colquitt refers the French aide-mémoire and Levant Japanese property question to Straus for action.
subfiles.summary: Adrian B. Colquitt of the Division of Near Eastern Affairs follows up on an afternoon telephone conversation with Oscar S. Straus in FC concerning the sequestration of Japanese property in Syria and Lebanon. Colquitt forwards the matter for appropriate action. He also notes that he requested the Translating Section to deliver the French aide-mémoire directly to Straus.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from NE to FC on Sequestration of Japanese Property in Syria and Lebanon

subfiles.about: Henderson reports his discussion with French Embassy Counselor Lacoste regarding French exclusion from Japanese property actions in the Levant.
subfiles.summary: Loy W. Henderson records that French Counselor Charles Lacoste presented French Aide-Mémoire No. 771 regarding Minister Wadsworth's failure to consult French authorities in Syria and Lebanon. Lacoste underscored French concern over the broader question of disposing of public and private Japanese property in neutral and non-belligerent nations. Henderson replied that he was unfamiliar with the operational details but promised to look into the matter and confer with Lacoste later.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Loy W. Henderson on Conversation with French Counselor Lacoste

subfiles.about: Routing slip directing correspondence on Japanese diplomatic archives to Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.summary: A brief State Department routing slip addressed to John Carter Vincent in FE, noting Mr. Lyon and the American Republics Area. It transmits the FC memorandum and attached newspaper clipping regarding diplomatic archives and General MacArthur's directives.
subfiles.title: Routing Slip to Far Eastern Affairs Regarding Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Lyon highlights difficulties caused by General MacArthur's delay in issuing archival surrender directives, enclosing a New York Times article.
subfiles.summary: Lyon emphasizes that a September 22 New York Times clipping from Stockholm illustrates the severe confusion resulting from General MacArthur's failure to order the Japanese Government to surrender diplomatic archives. The clipping reported that the Japanese Legation in Sweden was adding staff and promoting attachés even while ostensibly awaiting dissolution orders. Lyon notes that overseas missions are constantly requesting instructions and attaches a draft circular telegram informing them of the Tokyo delay.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from FC to FE Regarding Japanese Archives with New York Times Clipping

subfiles.about: Ambassador Simmons transmits an inventory receipt for Japanese archives delivered in San Salvador and notes the lack of confidential records.
subfiles.from: John F. Simmons (American Ambassador, San Salvador)
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Simmons reports that the Japanese archives in San Salvador, held by the Spanish Legation since December 1941, were delivered to the US Embassy via the Salvadoran Ministry of Foreign Relations. The archives contained no correspondence, codes, or personnel lists, which were presumed burned by Japanese diplomats upon departure in 1941. Simmons encloses an English translation of the receipt signed on August 27, 1945, listing office machines, motion picture films, phonograph discs, flags, abacos, and books.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 474 from San Salvador on Delivery of Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Despatch No. 474 from San Salvador to US military intelligence agencies and the FBI.
subfiles.summary: The State Department transmits copies of Despatch No. 474 from the American Embassy in San Salvador, dated September 28, 1945, to the Military Intelligence Division, the Office of Naval Intelligence, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The accompanying material details the recovered Japanese archives and property in El Salvador.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmittal of Despatch No. 474 from San Salvador
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, Federal Bureau of Investigation

subfiles.about: Straus reviews the policy reasons for excluding France from the Big Four archival seizures outside France, enclosing relevant telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Straus explains that Minister Wadsworth acted under instructions approved by Assistant Secretaries Julius Holmes and James Clement Dunn, which restricted archival seizures to the Big Four powers (US, UK, USSR, and China). While the Department agreed to include the French in custody of Japanese property within France itself (Deptel 4244 to Paris), expanding invitations elsewhere would trigger demands from other interested allies such as the Dutch and Australians. Straus encloses copies of Deptel 4244 of September 10 and the circular telegram of August 14, 1945, noting that action remains academic until MacArthur issues orders to Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on French Participation in Seizure of Japanese Archives with Attached Telegrams

subfiles.about: Acting Secretary Acheson advises diplomatic missions that instructions on Japanese archives remain delayed due to conditions in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Acheson informs all American diplomatic missions that the instructions anticipated in the circular telegram of August 29 have still not been issued due to the situation in Tokyo. The Department cannot provide further substantive instructions in the interim. Missions will be immediately informed by telegraph as soon as General MacArthur issues the surrender directives.
subfiles.title: Circular Telegram to All Diplomatic Missions on Delay in Tokyo Instructions

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Despatch No. 2857 from Panama containing a detailed Japanese archival inventory to intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State forwards copies of Despatch No. 2857 from the American Embassy in Panama, dated October 1, 1945, to the Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, and Federal Bureau of Investigation. The enclosure contains an extensive detailed inventory of Japanese records and intelligence material recovered in Panama.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmittal of Despatch No. 2857 from Panama
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, Federal Bureau of Investigation

subfiles.about: Donnelly transmits a comprehensive 27-page inventory of surviving Japanese Legation archives, card indexes, marked maps, and propaganda in Panama.
subfiles.from: Walter J. Donnelly (American Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Panama)
subfiles.summary: Walter J. Donnelly transmits a detailed inventory of the former Japanese Legation archives in Panama, supervised by Third Secretary V. Lansing Collins, Jr., with army linguists Sakoda and Nishioki, Embassy staff Pettis and Waters, and Chinese Legation Secretary Dr. Yen Shen Lu. The inventory details fifty empty binding folders, Japanese government gazettes (Kanpo), registers of military reservists and residents, an annotated military map of Panama highlighting Canal approaches and defense sites, and card indexes of hundreds of Japanese nationals. It also surveys extensive pre-war propaganda files and correspondence showing Japanese surveillance of Panamanian politics and US military movements prior to Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2857 from Panama Transmitting Detailed Inventory of Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Ambassador Norweb reports joint Allied examination of Japanese index cards in Havana and the need for an American Japanese-language expert.
subfiles.summary: Norweb reports that representatives of the American, British, Chinese, and Soviet missions inspected Japanese index cards held in Havana. The Cuban Ministry of State supplied a reliable unofficial translator, and the Chinese Legation Secretary is assisting in interpreting Chinese ideographs as distinct from kana. Norweb advises that if a detailed intelligence analysis of the cards is desired, a qualified American specialist in written Japanese will be necessary.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 631 from Habana Regarding Examination of Japanese Index Cards

subfiles.about: Lyon urges SWNCC action to obtain a directive from MacArthur and attaches a comprehensive global summary of archival status.
subfiles.summary: Lyon highlights the anomalous situation confronting US missions abroad because General MacArthur has failed to order the Japanese Government to surrender diplomatic archives, leaving Japanese diplomats unhindered in neutral capitals and protecting powers without authority to release files. Lyon urges that the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee (SWNCC) prompt the Joint Chiefs of Staff to issue an immediate directive ordering the recall of Japanese diplomats and the transfer of mission archives to US representatives acting for the Allies. An attached country-by-country survey as of October 2, 1945, details the archival status across dozens of posts from Addis Ababa to Wellington.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from FC to FE Urging SWNCC Directive to MacArthur with Worldwide Status Summary

subfiles.about: Ranken transmits a copy of a British Embassy telegram to London concerning US policy and MacArthur's objections.
subfiles.from: G. R. Ranken (Third Secretary, British Embassy, Washington)
subfiles.summary: G. R. Ranken forwards to Oscar S. Straus the text of a September 14, 1945, telegram sent by the British Embassy in Washington to the Foreign Office in London. The telegram reported that the State Department directed MacArthur to instruct Tokyo to turn over archives to the Four Powers, noted that MacArthur replied objecting to the suggested procedure, and observed that the US might be satisfied with mere access to archives if certain host nations insisted on retaining custody.
subfiles.title: British Embassy Compliments Slip Transmitting Telegram on State Department Policy

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State transmits photostatic copies of the Japanese map of Panama to the American Mission in Panama.
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes (Secretary of State, drafted by FC: PFCherp)
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State acknowledges receipt of Despatch No. 2918 of October 9, 1945, from the American Embassy in Panama. In accordance with the Embassy's request, the Department transmits under separate cover photostatic copies of the marked map of the Republic of Panama originally recovered from the former Japanese Legation archives.
subfiles.title: State Department Despatch to Panama Transmitting Copies of Japanese Map
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, Panama

subfiles.about: Collins requests seven photostatic copies of the marked Japanese map of Panama for military intelligence and Allied legations.
subfiles.from: V. Lansing Collins, Jr. (for Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Panama)
subfiles.summary: Collins refers to Despatch No. 2739 of September 19, 1945, and requests seven photostatic copies of the marked map of Panama found in the Japanese archives. He explains that copies are required for distribution to the Panamanian Government, the British and Chinese Legations, and local US intelligence services. He notes that the Assistant Chief of Staff for G-2, Panama Canal Department, and the District Intelligence Officer, 15th Naval District, both wish to conduct a thorough study of the map's markings.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2918 from Panama Requesting Copies of Japanese Map for Intelligence

subfiles.about: Straus clarifies to Ranken that US policy insists on full physical custody of Japanese archives rather than mere access.
subfiles.summary: Straus records his conversation with British Third Secretary G. R. Ranken to rectify a misunderstanding in the British Embassy's telegram of September 14 to London, which suggested the US would be content with access alone. Straus affirmed that official US policy demands full physical custody by the Four Allied Powers once MacArthur's orders are issued. They also discussed the situation in Argentina, where the American and British Ambassadors planned to obtain the archives directly from the Swiss Minister and confront the Argentine Government with a fait accompli; Ranken agreed to cable London requesting revised instructions.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Oscar Straus and G. R. Ranken on Archival Policy

subfiles.about: MacDonald inquires whether certain Japanese documents have been processed by the War Department and where they are located.
subfiles.from: J. E. MacDonald (Division of Economic Security Controls)
subfiles.summary: J. E. MacDonald follows up on a telephone conversation with Oscar S. Straus and attaches a description of specific Japanese papers of interest to the Division of Economic Security Controls. MacDonald clarifies that his division does not seek immediate physical possession of the documents, but wishes to ascertain their exact location and find out whether they have been processed by the War Department.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from ES to FC Inquiring About War Department Processing of Japanese Documents

subfiles.about: Straus provides Ranken with the draft text of the JCS message to MacArthur regarding surrender instructions for Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Straus meets with British Third Secretary G. R. Ranken to discuss the custody of Japanese archives. Straus informs Ranken that the Joint Chiefs of Staff requested General MacArthur, barring operational objections, to order the Japanese Government to surrender diplomatic and consular archives and property. Straus hands Ranken the text of the proposed directive, which outlines procedures for neutral countries, protecting powers, and Allied territories; Ranken expresses complete satisfaction that the instructions resolve London's prior concerns.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Oscar Straus and G. R. Ranken with JCS Directive Text

subfiles.about: Tittmann reports that his British colleague to the Holy See has now received formal instructions regarding Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Tittmann refers to his earlier telegram No. 195 concerning Japanese archives and property at the Vatican. He informs the Department that his British diplomatic colleague, who had previously joined in démarches on his own personal responsibility, received formal instructions by mail from London dated October 1 authorizing his participation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 208 from Vatican City on British Instructions Regarding Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: The British Embassy presents a comprehensive plan for Allied preservation, examination, and inter-Allied sharing of Japanese records worldwide.
subfiles.summary: The British Embassy submits a detailed five-page aide-mémoire emphasizing that Allied access to Japanese official and non-official records in Japan and abroad is essential for locating POWs and civilian internees, prosecuting war criminals, controlling disarmament, and identifying assets for reparations. It defines records comprehensively, urges orders forbidding destruction under severe penalties, and proposes that SCAP and theater commanders set up examination organizations. Great Britain requests the inclusion of British, Dominion, and Indian experts in Japan, proposes mechanisms to share intelligence among Allied governments, and asks if the US concurs and will instruct MacArthur accordingly.
subfiles.title: British Embassy Aide-Mémoire on Preservation and Examination of Japanese Records Worldwide

subfiles.about: Circular telegram transmitting the text of the JCS directive to MacArthur regarding instructions for the surrender of Japanese archives.
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes (Secretary of State, drafted by FC: OSStraus)
subfiles.summary: Secretary Byrnes informs all American diplomatic missions that the Joint Chiefs of Staff instructed General MacArthur, absent operational objections, to order the Japanese Government to surrender diplomatic and consular archives and property. The telegram quotes the full directive: in neutral states, Japanese missions must surrender archives to Four Power representatives while leaving protection of nationals to Sweden or Switzerland; in protecting power countries, physical custody goes to the Four Powers while routine protection continues; and in Allied nations, custody reverts to host governments with Big Four access. Missions are told that MacArthur is expected to act promptly.
subfiles.title: Circular Telegram to All Diplomatic Missions on JCS Directive to General MacArthur

subfiles.about: Byrnes instructs the Embassy in Buenos Aires to limit Swiss access to archives strictly to routine passport and visa files.
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes (Secretary of State, drafted by FC: PFCherp)
subfiles.summary: Secretary Byrnes telegraphs the American Embassy in Buenos Aires stating that following the transfer of Japanese archives, Swiss access must be strictly limited to necessary reference to passport and visa files or records of a similar routine nature. The cable adds that other procedural questions raised by the Embassy are addressed in the circular telegram of October 13 and an additional circular drafted that day.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1530 to Buenos Aires on Limiting Swiss Access to Archives

subfiles.about: Byrnes authorizes accepting access rather than custody for archives in Mexico if Allied colleagues agree, or temporary joint Four Power receipt.
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes (Secretary of State, drafted by FC: PFCherp)
subfiles.summary: Secretary Byrnes advises the American Embassy in Mexico City that the Department will be satisfied with access to Japanese archives as proposed in Despatch 26,919, provided the British, Soviet, and Chinese representatives concur and the Swedish Legation agrees. If the Swedes insist on transferring the archives to the Four Powers while the Mexican Foreign Office objects, the Department is prepared as an exception to receive them jointly and immediately transfer custody to the Mexican Foreign Office.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1679 to Mexico City on Transfer and Access to Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Shaw reports that Spain released Japanese Legation property in Quito to Ecuador, notes an unopened safe, and transmits inventories.
subfiles.from: Geo. P. Shaw (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Quito)
subfiles.summary: Shaw reports that authorized by Madrid, the Spanish Minister turned over the Japanese archives and property left in Spanish custody in April 1942 to the Ecuadoran Ministry for Foreign Affairs. Inspection showed only routine office furnishings, a few Japanese books, and two protocol folders, with the exception of an unopened Remington office safe whose combination was not provided by Japanese Chargé Nagumo. Shaw encloses Spanish and English copies of the 1942 turnover inventory signed by Gómez-Acebo and Nagumo, and requests instructions on whether to demand custody from Ecuador and how to open the safe.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3560 from Quito on Release of Japanese Archives and Property in Ecuador

subfiles.about: Cabot reports plans to terminate leases on Japanese premises in Belgrano, rent downtown space, intern Chancellor Tani, and manage Swiss access.
subfiles.from: John M. Cabot (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Buenos Aires)
subfiles.summary: Cabot reports on operational arrangements in Buenos Aires in light of the circular telegram of October 13. To accommodate Swiss routine protection of Japanese nationals while Allied powers hold custody of archives, the Embassy plans to terminate leases on the ex-Japanese residence and office in Belgrano, lease a downtown office for Allied examination and Swiss access, and request the internment of Japanese Chancellor Tani to be replaced by a vetted translator. Cabot requests instructions on the permissible extent of Swiss access and confirms British concurrence.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2533 from Buenos Aires on Arrangements for Japanese Archives and Swiss Representation

subfiles.about: Internal note approving the forwarding of Collins's detailed Panama archival report.
subfiles.summary: An informal handwritten note from RPH in the Foreign Activity Correlation Division to Thomas C. Mann in Special Political Affairs. RPH states that following their conversation, there is no harm or objection in forwarding Third Secretary Collins's essay and detailed inventory regarding the Japanese archives in Panama.
subfiles.title: Internal Note to Mr. Mann Regarding Forwarding Collins's Panama Inventory

subfiles.about: Straus attaches a copy of the British telegram to London and his memorandum for Clattenburg.
subfiles.summary: An informal note from Oscar S. Straus in FC to Albert E. Clattenburg, Jr. in the Special War Problems Division (SWP). Straus attaches a copy of the telegram sent by the British Embassy to London regarding Japanese archives, together with his own memorandum on the topic, and notes that the matter was taken up directly with Mr. Ranken.
subfiles.title: Internal Note from Oscar Straus to Albert Clattenburg Regarding British Telegram
